剣 concerns a sword or blade, especially a double-edged sword. The word 剣 つるぎ can also name swords more broadly; do not treat "double-edged" as an exceptionless definition.

Modern-shape mnemonic, not etymology: Picture a sword beside a pointed roof, a horizontal line and a 口-shaped box, with spreading strokes below. The sword-shaped part is the right-hand 刂. This invented scene helps distinguish the modern shape; it is not a historical or phonetic explanation.

Both source readings are selected for reading questions. The standalone noun 剣 can also be read けん; that does not make every dictionary sense interchangeable between the two pronunciations.
剣 つるぎ — sword; especially a double-edged blade
真剣 しんけん — serious; earnest; also a real sword rather than a wooden practice weapon
剣道 けんどう — kendo, the martial art using bamboo swords

The indexing radical is 刀, visible here as 刂. 剛, "sturdy; unyielding strength," 剖, "dissect; split open," and 則, "rule; follow a model," share right-hand 刂 but have different left blocks and meanings.
刀 かたな especially suggests a Japanese single-edged sword; 剣 especially suggests a double-edged one. Broader sword uses overlap, so this is not a strict division of all swords.
刃 は focuses on the blade or cutting edge, rather than naming the whole sword.
真剣 usually describes earnest engagement in the examples on its word card. Do not translate every occurrence literally as a weapon, or use it for every English sense of "serious."

剣 つるぎ — sword; especially a double-edged blade
剣 is a noun for a sword, especially a double-edged one. This article teaches つるぎ. Dictionaries also recognize broader sword usage, so the double-edged association is not an absolute restriction.
博物館で古い剣を見ました。 (はくぶつかんでふるいつるぎをみました。) — I saw an old sword at the museum.
これは剣の写真です。 (これはつるぎのしゃしんです。) — This is a photograph of a sword.
In 剣を見る (つるぎをみる), "look at a sword," を marks the object. 剣の写真 uses の to connect the sword with its photograph.
剣 represents the whole native noun つるぎ here. There is no compound to split. The same spelling also has the word reading けん; this is another valid pronunciation, not a correction of つるぎ.

刀 かたな especially suggests a Japanese single-edged sword, while 剣 つるぎ especially suggests a double-edged one. These associations do not partition every broader use of "sword." 日本刀 にほんとう identifies the Japanese sword tradition.

刃 は, "blade; cutting edge," focuses on a cutting part. ナイフ, "knife," and 包丁 ほうちょう, "kitchen knife," name different kinds of tools, not general translations of つるぎ. There is no natural lexical antonym.

真剣 しんけん has a literal noun sense "real sword," contrasting with a wooden practice weapon, as well as its familiar "serious; earnest" adjective sense. Do not infer the meaning of the whole compound just by translating 剣.
JMdict restricts its separate bayonet, swordsmanship and zoological senses to the reading けん. Those are not additional senses to memorize for this つるぎ article.

真 contributes "true; real," and 剣 means "sword." The compound also has the literal noun sense "a real sword," as opposed to a wooden practice weapon. That literal contrast is a useful association, not a reason to translate a serious discussion as a weapon.
